doc.title: Bobby Militello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 14, 2002

title: Jazz in schools and young audiences
summary: Schools have exposed generations to jazz, and Brubeck concerts sell out with young listeners.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Has it become more of an art music? I’m not sure I’m saying that right but it’s been culturally certainly elevated and it’s in all the schools now and you know you can go to universities and stuff.

Well that’s the reason why I think it’s growing — it’s actually growing. It’s getting bigger all the time. Because the schools have had this music in it since I was in grammar school. So its effect is taking hold and that is a whole series of two generations, maybe three generations of kids have now been exposed to jazz in school, and of those kids maybe only let’s say three percent of them really dig it and that’s their mainstay music.

But they all have an appreciation for it, because they all played the big band swing tunes in high school bands, and they all played whatever fusion charts and everything were written, you know, Bob Mintzer charts and all the other things — they all played all this stuff. So they have an appreciation for it. And they come out to see the gigs now. And they come out to see the players. They enjoy doing that and they’re open to being exposed to jazz. I think you’re seeing more people, we sell out everything with Dave. I mean on a scale of one to ten, nine point five of the gigs are completely sold out. Full of kids. Kids coming up to me all the time. I heard your solo on this and I heard your solo on that and wow what this is and what that is. And these are kids and this is an 82 year old guy. It used to be, a while ago, when I first started with Dave 21 years ago, sometimes you’d meet a kid who didn’t know who Dave Brubeck was because it was an extension of an era. I mean we moved a shift there and this kid was before that. But very seldom do you meet anybody who doesn’t know who Brubeck is now. And the amount of kids again, that are exposed — I think we’ve got a growth of jazz that is wonderful in the United States. I don’t think it’s negative in any way, shape or form. The only thing that’s negative about it is the people who write about it and talk about it and that kind of thing, who perceive it still as the underground and why can’t jazz do so much better. I mean jeez — guys like Sonny Rollins and anybody who’s been around for a long time are making great bread out there right now. They’re doing fine. They’re selling out everything that they do. They can’t work enough gigs. Brubeck right now, we turn down almost as much as we take.
